New GPS Model Predicts Where Massive Earthquakes Will Strike: Inside the UC Riverside Breakthrough

UC Riverside geophysicists developed a groundbreaking GPS algorithm that pinpoints where mega-earthquakes strike, validated by the Kamchatka rupture. Here is how the strain-mapping model works.

✍️ By: Geophysics & Earth Science Research Desk 📅 Published: September 7, 2026 ⏱️ Read Time: 6 min read

1.The Century-Old Quest: Decoding Fault Locking Before the Rupture

For decades, predicting earthquakes has been considered the holy grail of geophysics. While seismologists can reliably estimate the statistical probability of a seismic event over a thirty-year window, pinpointing the precise location where a fault will tear open has remained an unsolved scientific challenge.

Now, a breakthrough study published in Geophysical Research Letters by geophysicists at the University of California, Riverside (UCR) suggests a major turning point.

Led by UCR researchers Axelle Perriollat and Gareth Funning, the team developed an algorithmic method that analyzes minute millimeter-scale surface deformations captured by GPS stations to extract the exact segments of a fault that are locked, accumulating dangerous tectonic strain, and primed to rupture.

The model underwent an extraordinary real-world validation: it had independently identified the precise fault patch beneath Russia's remote Kamchatka Peninsula before it ruptured in a colossal magnitude-8.8 subduction earthquake.

2.Mapping Fault "Asperities": How the Inversion Model Works

Tectonic plates do not slide past one another smoothly. Instead, along massive subduction zones—where one heavy oceanic plate dives beneath a lighter continental plate—immense friction creates locked patches known as asperities.

• Silent Strain Accumulation: While a fault appears quiet on the surface, locked asperities grip together while the surrounding plates continue moving, warping the overlying crust. • GPS Deformation Tracking: The UCR algorithm extracts subtle, ongoing directional changes from surface GPS sensors, converting that ground warping into an inverted friction map of the fault deep underground. • Identifying the Breaking Point: Rather than guessing when a rupture will happen, the model isolates precisely which structural patch has absorbed enough elastic stress to cause an imminent, catastrophic slip.

"Earthquakes make headlines when they happen, but the fault has been quietly accumulating stress for years beforehand," explained co-author Gareth Funning. "This strain can be measured."

3.Tested by Reality: The Kamchatka Subduction Zone Validation

The researchers initially tested their algorithm on a relatively limited historical GPS dataset collected along the Pacific coast of the Kamchatka Peninsula.

When a massive magnitude-8.8 earthquake ruptured the plate boundary, post-event seismic analysis confirmed that the primary slip aligned directly with the locked asperity their algorithm had mapped in advance.

The study also shed light on why seismic hazards vary over time. While Kamchatka previously experienced a magnitude-9.0 earthquake in 1952 that spawned a massive trans-oceanic tsunami, the recent rupture generated a significantly smaller tsunami wave. The UCR data revealed that the shallowest, seafloor-adjacent portion of the fault slipped far less this time, demonstrating that identical fault lines release accumulated stress differently across centuries.

4.What the Model Can—and Cannot—Do: Demarcating Science from Sensation

While the study marks a major leap forward for geological hazard mapping, the authors are careful to debunk sensationalized claims of immediate "earthquake prediction":

1. Location vs. Timing: The model identifies where stress has concentrated to dangerous levels, but it cannot forecast the exact date, week, or hour of a rupture. 2. Tsunami Sizing: The algorithm maps locked patches in the crust, but cannot currently calculate the exact vertical displacement of the seafloor required to predict precise tsunami heights. 3. Public Preparedness Remains Paramount: Funning stressed that hazard mapping should complement, not replace, disaster resilience: "Especially where we live in Southern California, the question isn’t whether it will happen, but when. There is no substitute for preparation."

5.Expanding to California's Hayward Fault & Global Pacific Subduction Zones

Following the success of the Kamchatka test, the research team is scaling the algorithm to evaluate major subduction zones and fault networks around the world:

• California Faults: Researchers are testing the algorithm along the Hayward Fault in the San Francisco Bay Area, which exhibits a complex patchwork of silently creeping sections alongside dangerously locked zones capable of producing devastating urban earthquakes. • Global Subduction Zones: The model is being calibrated for high-risk zones across Japan, Chile, Mexico, New Zealand, and the Pacific Northwest's Cascadia Subduction Zone. • Bridging the Offshore Data Gap: The primary technical hurdle remains offshore monitoring. Because GPS signals cannot penetrate seawater, scientists rely on emerging seafloor acoustic transponders and newly launched radar satellites to map faults that lie hundreds of miles offshore beneath the ocean.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Q1: Can scientists predict the exact time of an earthquake?

No. Current geophysical tools cannot predict the exact day or time an earthquake will strike. The UC Riverside model instead pinpoints the specific fault patches where stress is accumulating and where a rupture is most likely to occur.

Q2: How does GPS detect earthquake zones?

Networked GPS stations measure minuscule, millimeter-level ground movements over months and years. When a fault is stuck, the surrounding rock warps and buckles, creating a distinct movement pattern on the surface that computers can decode.

Q3: Is California's Hayward Fault in danger of a major rupture?

The Hayward Fault is heavily locked in several urban segments beneath the East Bay. Seismologists actively monitor its creeping and locked boundaries, and the new model aims to identify the specific segments carrying the highest accumulated strain.
